rv.q: So blistering is her performance in Luke Norris’s pregnancy drama that if the Royal Court Theatre could plug her into the National Grid, it would save a fortune on its energy bills for the duration of the run.
This is a tear-jerker with 100% heart, 0% sentimentality.

A special talent, ferocious and funny, tragicomedy incarnate: directed by Jeremy Herrin, who led Denise Gough in a career-changing role in People, Places﻿ and Things, Sheehy can add to her credits (The Brightening Air, Machinal﻿) another astonishing feat.
A generous, humane play, Guess How Much I Love You? is a fine start to the Royal Court’s 70th anniversary season.
The two central performances are extraordinary.
I can’t exactly call the play a pleasure to watch but it’s definitely a privilege.

For all its overpowering bleakness, there’s something ultimately hopeful about Norris’s play, and the way that he details every hideous contour of this pair’s suffering – then shows us that this, too, is survivable.
And yet this smartly observed, cannily constructed, beautifully performed play will stay with me.

Norris isn’t trying to show a balanced account of what parenthood typically does to a couple, but rather the dark places it can go. Most parents are liable to experience a bit of what this pair experience – but theirs is the uncut form. But even accepting it’s a relief to have not been entirely in their boat, Guess How Much I Love You?
It’s as impressive as the dissection of human heartbreak is flawless.
Yet while Norris is clearly motivated by the need to tell a ghastly story that could affect any prospective parent, his subject feels like a creative cop-out.
Everyone who values a good night out should approach with caution.
I would still urge everyone who is able, to attend a performance of Guess How Much I Love You?
Gutturally affecting, this is theatre that paints a vivid picture of the delicacy of being alive.
This is a play full of feeling with no phoney sentiment but movingly real, except perhaps for its final scene which could be both a remembered dream or one for the future.
The writing is vividly realistic, accurate in its depiction of extreme emotions, and profoundly compassionate in its feelings for the couple, which are intended be Everyman and Everywoman.
Luke Norris’ writing also deserves praise, with its unerring ability to keep pulling the rug from under you.
The play is superbly written, never losing either its tension, its humour or its ability to involve the audience in this searing set of choices.
This is a beautiful play that acknowledges the human cost and resilience in tragedy.
Guess How Much I Love You? is witty and funny yet emotionally disturbing and heartbreaking – an unusual combination that is executed exceptionally.
It is they who make the play and Jeremy Herrin’s production special.
This production comes close, but its relentless conflict too often keeps the audience at a frustrated distance.

cn.t: A harrowing but acclaimed drama about a couple facing an impossible choice after a devastating scan. Critics praise exceptional performances from Sheehy and Aramayo, though some find it emotionally manipulative.
